summary: A country in northwestern South America facing both the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean, known for coffee, biodiversity and the novelist García Márquez.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism arrived with the Spanish landing on the Colombian coast in 1499 and the founding of Bogotá in 1538, and in the colonial period it was closely bound to the Spanish crown; Cartagena even had an Inquisition tribunal (1610). The 1886 constitution declared Catholicism the state religion, and in 1887 a concordat was signed with the Vatican, giving the Church privileges in education and marriage. The new constitution of 1991 established freedom of religion and the separation of church and state, but Catholicism remains the largest religion today.

ranking.name: Protestantism (Evangelical)
ranking.description: Protestantism was introduced in the mid-19th century by American Presbyterian missionaries, but was persecuted during the mid-20th-century period of 'La Violencia' (1948–1958). After the 1991 constitution guaranteed freedom of religion, Pentecostal and Evangelical churches grew rapidly, especially on the urban periphery and in areas affected by armed conflict, attracting followers through community mutual aid and faith healing, and their share has risen to about 17%.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious population has grown in recent decades, concentrated mainly among the young generation and the highly educated in large cities such as Bogotá and Medellín. After the 1991 constitution established the separation of church and state, society gradually secularized, and issues such as the legalization of same-sex marriage in 2016 have also led some people to distance themselves from the church.

ranking.name: Other
ranking.description: Other religions include Judaism, Islam, Jehovah's Witnesses and the traditional beliefs of indigenous peoples. Muslims are mainly descendants of Lebanese and Syrian immigrants who moved to Caribbean coastal cities (such as Maicao and Barranquilla) in the 19th–20th centuries; indigenous peoples such as the Kogi of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta still maintain their own cosmology and priestly traditions.

religion.background: Before the arrival of the Spanish, indigenous peoples of Colombia such as the Muisca worshipped the sun and moon, and the famous legend of 'El Dorado' originates in the gold-offering ceremony the Muisca held at Lake Guatavita. After the Spanish conquest in the 16th century, Catholicism became the official religion of the colony. After independence in 1819, Liberals and Conservatives were long at odds over the role of the Church, and the 1886 constitution established Catholicism as the state religion. The new constitution of 1991 implemented the separation of church and state, and the Evangelical and non-religious populations have gradually grown.

language.official: The official language is Spanish, and indigenous languages are also official within their territories.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: Spanish arrived with Spanish colonization in the 16th century; in the colonial period it was the language of administration, the Church and education, and it became the national language after independence in 1819. Colombian Spanish, especially the accent around Bogotá, is often regarded as clearly pronounced and formal in usage. Because the indigenous population fell greatly in the colonial period, Spanish has become the mother tongue of about 99% of the population.

ranking.name: Indigenous languages (Wayuu and more than 60 others)
ranking.description: Colombia has more than 60 indigenous languages, of which Wayuu, in the northern Guajira Peninsula, has the most speakers, with several hundred thousand; others include many languages of the Amazon region and the Andes. The 1991 constitution recognized indigenous languages as official within their territories, and the Mother Tongue Law of 2010 protects indigenous and Creole languages, but many languages still face the danger of disappearing because of their few speakers.

language.history: Before the arrival of the Spanish, Colombia had hundreds of indigenous languages, and the Chibcha language used by the Muisca was the main language of the eastern Andean plateau. After Spanish colonization in the 16th century, Spanish became the dominant language, and in 1770 King Charles III of Spain ordered the promotion of Spanish and restrictions on indigenous languages. After independence in 1819, Spanish became the national language. The new constitution of 1991 recognized Colombia as a multiethnic and multicultural country, and indigenous languages, the Creole English of the San Andrés islands and the Palenquero language of Palenque are all protected.

ranking.name: Bandeja paisa
ranking.description: A hearty platter on one large plate including rice, red beans, ground beef, fried pork rind, sausage, fried egg, fried plantain, avocado and arepa.
ranking.history: Bandeja paisa originates from the farmers and mule-train transport workers of Antioquia Province (whose people are called 'paisas'), who from the 19th century cleared coffee plantations in the mountains and needed high-calorie food to cope with heavy labor. Almost all of the ingredients on the platter come from local farms. Today it is regarded as the signature dish of Colombia; in 2005 the government moved to designate it the national dish, but the proposal provoked controversy because the portion is too large and it is not representative enough.

ranking.name: Arepa
ranking.description: A round, flat cake made from white corn flour, cooked on a griddle, which can be filled with cheese, meat or egg, crisp outside and soft inside.
ranking.history: The arepa is a traditional indigenous food of Colombia and Venezuela that existed before the Spanish arrived, made by the indigenous peoples by grinding corn on stone. Colombia has different versions in different places, such as the fried egg arepa (arepa de huevo) of the Caribbean coast and the thin white arepa of Antioquia. It is the staple of Colombian breakfasts and snacks, and Colombians and Venezuelans often argue over which is the arepa's 'birthplace'.

ranking.name: Ajiaco (Bogotá chicken soup)
ranking.description: A thick soup stewed from chicken, three different kinds of potatoes, corn and guascas herb, served with cream, capers and avocado added.
ranking.history: Ajiaco is the signature dish of the capital, Bogotá, combining the indigenous potatoes and corn with the chicken brought by the Spanish. Bogotá lies on a plateau at an elevation of about 2,600 meters with a cool climate, and hot soup is part of local daily meals. Guasca is a wild Andean herb that adds a distinctive flavor to the soup and is regarded as a symbol of Bogotá culture.
ranking.imageCredit: Mauricio Giraldo from Bogotá, Colombia・CC BY-SA 2.0・Wikimedia Commons

ranking.name: Sancocho
ranking.description: A thick soup of meat (chicken, beef, fish and so on) stewed for a long time with cassava, plantain, yam and corn, with versions varying from place to place.
ranking.history: Sancocho is found all over Latin America and is generally thought to derive from the stew tradition of Spain and the Canary Islands, brought with Spanish colonists after the 16th century and combined with the root vegetables of African slaves and indigenous peoples. In Colombia, the Caribbean coast makes the soup with fish, while the interior uses chicken or beef. It is a classic dish of weekend family gatherings and riverside picnics, often cooked in a big pot over a wood fire.

ranking.name: Lechona (roast whole pig)
ranking.description: A whole pig is deboned and stuffed with rice, peas, onion and pork, then roasted in an earth oven for more than ten hours, with crisp skin and a juicy filling.
ranking.history: Lechona is a traditional dish of Tolima Department; in the colonial period the Spanish brought pigs to the Americas and combined them with local rice and spices. Because it requires a whole pig and long roasting, it is usually prepared for large gatherings such as festivals, weddings and Christmas. It is especially common at festivals in Tolima and surrounding departments and is also regarded as a representative festive dish of Colombia's interior.
